fuentes/tablillas-de-cnosos/autor.texto: Scribes of the palace of Knossos

fuentes/tablillas-de-cnosos/resumen.texto: Archive of Linear B tablets found by Evans from 1900 in the palace of Knossos, the oldest and most numerous set of texts in that script. They record stocks, flocks, textiles and weapons of the palace. Their date is disputed: Evans put them around 1400 BC and others, such as Palmer, around 1200 BC.

fuentes/tablillas-de-cnosos/por_que_impo.texto: They show that Knossos was administered in Mycenaean Greek, which places the Mycenaeans in the palace after the end of the Minoan palaces of Crete; their decipherment served to read the rest of the corpus.

fuentes/tablillas-de-tebas/autor.texto: Scribes of the palace of Thebes

fuentes/tablillas-de-tebas/resumen.texto: Linear B tablets found on the Cadmea, the acropolis of Thebes in Boeotia, which record offerings, personnel and palace goods. The fire that destroyed the building preserved them.

fuentes/tablillas-de-tebas/por_que_impor.texto: They prove that Thebes was the seat of a palace with its own administration, like Pylos, Mycenae and Knossos.

fuentes/tablillas-de-micenas/resumen.texto: Linear B tablets found since 1950 in buildings of the Mycenae citadel, with lists of goods and people. They were preserved when the fire that destroyed the buildings baked them.

fuentes/tablillas-de-micenas/por_que_imp.texto: They confirm that Mycenae had a written administration, like the other palace centers.

fuentes/tablillas-de-tirinto/resumen.texto: A few Linear B tablets found at Tiryns, with records of goods, showing writing at a center near Mycenae.

fuentes/tablillas-de-tirinto/por_que_imp.texto: They show that palace writing was not confined to the four largest centers.

fuentes/tablilla-py-ta-641/autor.texto: Scribe of the palace of Pylos

fuentes/tablilla-py-ta-641/resumen.texto: Tablet found by Blegen in 1952 at Pylos, listing vessels, tripods and cups, with their shapes drawn next to their names in Linear B. It was written around 1180 BC by the scribe known as «Hand 2», perhaps Phugebris. The drawings of the vessels helped Ventris check his reading of the script.

fuentes/tablilla-py-ta-641/por_que_impor.texto: It is cited as the most famous tablet from Pylos, because its ideograms showed that the signs transcribed Greek words.

fuentes/textos-en-lineal-a/resumen.texto: Corpus of Linear A texts, the script of Minoan Crete c. 1800–1450 BC, with tablets found at Agia Triada, Zakros, Phaistos, Knossos and other sites, and with inscriptions on vessels and cult objects. The numbers and some logograms can be read, but the language remains unidentified and the system is not deciphered.

fuentes/textos-en-lineal-a/por_que_impor.texto: It is the written record of the Minoan world, and the basis of the script that the Mycenaeans adapted to Greek as Linear B.

fuentes/disco-de-festos/resumen.texto: Disc of baked clay with signs stamped in a spiral on both faces, found in 1908 by the Italian mission at Phaistos, in the storeroom of a palace building. It is dated to Middle Minoan III; it is not known what language or writing system it transcribes, or whether it is genuine or a unique original.

fuentes/disco-de-festos/por_que_importa.texto: It is an isolated and undeciphered object of Minoan writing, with signs different from those of Linear A.

fuentes/jeroglificos-cretenses/resumen.texto: Hieroglyphic script of Crete, used on stone seals and in clay during the period of the first palaces, between c. 2000 and 1700 BC. A few texts survive, most of them on seals; the script is not deciphered.

fuentes/jeroglificos-cretenses/por_que_i.texto: It is the oldest writing of Crete, earlier than Linear A.

fuentes/hacha-de-arkalochori/resumen.texto: Votive axe with an inscription of some fifteen signs, found in the Arkalochori cave, which mixes signs of Linear A and of other Minoan scripts. Its reading is not known.

fuentes/hacha-de-arkalochori/por_que_imp.texto: It is one of the longest and most debated inscriptions in the undeciphered Minoan corpus.

fuentes/mascara-de-agamenon/resumen.texto: Gold funerary mask found by Schliemann in 1876 in Shaft Grave V of Grave Circle A at Mycenae. It is dated to the 16th century BC, some three centuries before the time of the Agamemnon of epic. Its authenticity has been debated: at the end of the 20th and beginning of the 21st century William M. Calder III and David Traill questioned it and proposed that Schliemann had it made by a forger, while other specialists defend it as ancient.

fuentes/mascara-de-agamenon/por_que_impo.texto: It is the best-known object from the shaft graves of Mycenae and a symbol of Schliemann's archaeology.

fuentes/panoplia-de-dendra/resumen.texto: Armor of fifteen pieces of bronze plates, with a cuirass, shoulder guards, greaves and forearm protection, found in 1960 in a chamber tomb at Dendra. It is dated to the late 15th century BC and is the oldest known beaten-metal cuirass from Greece.

fuentes/panoplia-de-dendra/por_que_impor.texto: It shows how a Mycenaean warrior was equipped, and its drawing reappears as an ideogram on tablets from Knossos, Pylos and Tiryns.

fuentes/agata-del-combate-de-pilos/resum.texto: Agate seal with a combat scene of three warriors, found in 2015 in the Griffin Warrior tomb, next to the palace of Nestor. It is in Minoan style and its detail is exceptional.

fuentes/agata-del-combate-de-pilos/por_q.texto: It shows how close the Mycenaean ruling groups were to Minoan art around 1450 BC.

fuentes/copas-de-vafio/resumen.texto: Two gold cups with scenes of bull capture, found in 1889 by Tsountas in the tholos tomb of Vapheio, in Laconia. They are considered Minoan art or the work of mainland Greek workshops with Minoan influence.

fuentes/copas-de-vafio/por_que_importa.texto: They document the influence of Crete on mainland Greece in the Late Helladic period.

fuentes/vaso-de-los-segadores/resumen.texto: Steatite rhyton with a procession of men carrying farm tools, found in the villa of Agia Triada. It is one of the best-known objects of Minoan art from the Neopalatial period.

fuentes/vaso-de-los-segadores/por_que_im.texto: It shows a collective scene of Minoan society in Late Minoan IA.

fuentes/vaso-de-los-guerreros/resumen.texto: Painted Mycenaean krater, found by Schliemann at Mycenae, with a procession of warriors with helmets, shields and spears and a woman who bids farewell. It is dated to Late Helladic IIIC.

fuentes/vaso-de-los-guerreros/por_que_im.texto: It is one of the few painted images of Mycenaean warriors on pottery.

fuentes/puerta-de-los-leones-fuente/resu.texto: Relief of two lionesses resting on a column, above the lintel of the main entrance to the Mycenae citadel, c. 1250 BC. It is the only surviving monumental Mycenaean sculpture and the largest from the Aegean Bronze Age. Pausanias saw it in the 2nd century.

fuentes/puerta-de-los-leones-fuente/por_.texto: It documents Mycenaean monumental architecture and its iconography of power.

fuentes/anillo-de-nestor/resumen.texto: Gold signet ring that Evans described in 1925 and which, according to him, came from a tholos near Pylos; it is in the Ashmolean in Oxford. Its authenticity is disputed: some regard it as a modern forgery and others as ancient.

fuentes/anillo-de-nestor/por_que_importa.texto: It shows a cult scene in Minoan style; its disputed authenticity makes it a case for caution with pieces lacking an excavation context.

fuentes/palacio-de-minos-evans/titulo.texto: The Palace of Minos at Knossos

fuentes/palacio-de-minos-evans/resumen.texto: Report by Arthur Evans on his excavations at Knossos, in four volumes published between 1921 and 1935. It sets the Minoan sequence in three periods and presents his reconstruction of the palace as that of a priest-king, an interpretation that many archaeologists dispute.

fuentes/palacio-de-minos-evans/por_que_i.texto: It is the foundational work of Minoan archaeology and the source of its basic terms, although its reconstructions and chronology have been revised.

fuentes/documents-in-mycenaean-greek/res.texto: 1956 book by Michael Ventris and John Chadwick with the reading and commentary of the Linear B tablets. It fixes the value of the signs and presents a selection of texts with their interpretation.

fuentes/documents-in-mycenaean-greek/por.texto: It is the exposition of the 1952 decipherment and the basis for reading the Mycenaean texts.

fuentes/the-pylos-tablets-bennett/resume.texto: Edition of the Pylos tablets by Emmett L. Bennett Jr., 1951. It orders the signs of Linear B and their use, so that other researchers could attempt to read the script.

fuentes/the-pylos-tablets-bennett/por_qu.texto: It gave Ventris and Chadwick the material for the decipherment.

fuentes/the-mycenaean-pottery-furumark/r.texto: Three-volume work by Arne Furumark on Mycenaean pottery. It defines the classes and phases of the Late Helladic period and their relative chronology.

fuentes/the-mycenaean-pottery-furumark/p.texto: Its phases remain the basis of the relative chronology of the Aegean Late Bronze Age.

fuentes/the-arts-in-prehistoric-greece-h.texto: Sinclair Hood's handbook on Aegean Bronze Age art, from the Cyclades to Mycenae.
Its review called it the standard reference handbook on Aegean art.

fuentes/cambridge-ancient-history-egeo/t.texto: The Cambridge Ancient History (volumes on the Aegean in the Bronze Age)

fuentes/cambridge-ancient-history-egeo/r.texto: Collective synthesis of ancient history, whose second edition devotes volumes to the Bronze Age in the Aegean, with the relative and absolute chronology of Crete, the Cyclades and mainland Greece.

fuentes/cambridge-ancient-history-egeo/p.texto: It is an academic synthesis reference for the period, cited for its chronologies.

fuentes/catalogo-de-las-naves/soporte.texto: Passage from Book II of the Iliad

fuentes/catalogo-de-las-naves/resumen.texto: List in Book II of the Iliad of the Greek contingents that went to Troy, with their leaders, their ships and the places they came from. Several of the places it names, such as Pylos, Tiryns and Mycenae, have Mycenaean occupation; others have not been identified with certainty.

fuentes/catalogo-de-las-naves/por_que_im.texto: It is the epic passage most often contrasted with the geography of Mycenaean Greece.

fuentes/carga-del-pecio-de-uluburun/auto.texto: Crew and merchants of the ship

fuentes/carga-del-pecio-de-uluburun/resu.texto: Remains of a ship about 15 m long, sunk at the end of the 14th century BC south of Kaş, in Turkey, with more than 20 tons of cargo: copper and tin ingots, terebinth resin, painted pottery and raw glass, as well as luxury objects and personal belongings. It was excavated between 1984 and 1994.

fuentes/carga-del-pecio-de-uluburun/por_.texto: It shows the trade in metals and luxury goods among the Aegean, Cyprus, the Levant and Egypt in the Late Bronze Age.

fuentes/carga-del-pecio-de-cabo-gelidony.texto: Cargo of the Cape Gelidonya shipwreck
Crew and merchants of the ship

Late Bronze Age shipwreck, c. 1200 BC, found in 1954 at Cape Gelidonya, on the south coast of Anatolia, and excavated from 1960 by Throckmorton, Bass and Du Plat Taylor. It was the oldest known shipwreck until the discovery of Uluburun.
It was one of the first projects that gave rise to nautical archaeology.

fuentes/sellos-minoicos/soporte.texto: Seals carved in stone and other materials

fuentes/sellos-minoicos/resumen.texto: Impression seals the size of a fingernail, carved in stone, metal or ivory, found in quantity at Knossos, Malia and Phaistos. They were used to mark documents and objects and as personal amulets; they bear images and, on some, Cretan hieroglyphs.

fuentes/sellos-minoicos/por_que_importa.texto: They are the basis for the study of Minoan iconography and administration.

fuentes/ceramica-de-kamares/resumen.texto: Minoan pottery style, with light decoration on a dark ground in white, red and orange motifs, which appeared in Middle Minoan IA, around 2100 BC, and lasted until Late Minoan IA, around 1450 BC. It has also been found in the Levant and in Egypt.

fuentes/ceramica-de-kamares/por_que_impo.texto: It allows Minoan strata to be dated and Cretan trade to be traced.

fuentes/figurillas-cicladicas/resumen.texto: Marble figurines, mostly standing females with arms folded, produced in the Cyclades during the Early Cycladic period. Many were removed without a record of their context. Some keep traces of paint on the flat face.

fuentes/figurillas-cicladicas/por_que_im.texto: They are the best-known expression of Cycladic culture.

fuentes/principe-de-los-lirios/resumen.texto: Painted relief found in fragments in the palace of Knossos, dated by Hood to around 1550 BC, in Late Minoan IA. Today it is in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum, largely reconstructed.

fuentes/principe-de-los-lirios/por_que_i.texto: It is one of the best-known Minoan paintings, and the subject of debate about how it was reconstructed.

fuentes/casco-de-colmillos-de-jabali/res.texto: Helmet made of boar's tusk plates fixed to a base of leather and felt. Known from the shaft graves of Mycenae, of the 18th or 17th century BC, to Elateia, in the 10th century BC. The Iliad describes one that Meriones gives to Odysseus.

fuentes/casco-de-colmillos-de-jabali/por.texto: It documents Mycenaean armament and its memory in epic poetry.

fuentes/sarcofago-de-agia-triada/resumen.texto: Limestone sarcophagus 137 cm long, dated to around 1400 BC or a few decades later, found in 1903 in a chamber tomb at Agia Triada. It is the only object with a series of narrative scenes of a Minoan funerary ritual, and it is now in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum.

fuentes/sarcofago-de-agia-triada/por_que.texto: It is cited as a figurative source for the Late Minoan funerary ritual.

fuentes/estatuillas-de-la-diosa-de-las-s.texto: Two incomplete figurines found in 1903 in the palace of Knossos, from around 1600 BC, towards the end of the Neopalatial period. Evans restored them and drew from them ideas about a snake goddess that later criticism considers excessive and speculative.
They are among the most reproduced objects of Minoan civilization and an example of the debates over Evans's restorations.

fuentes/saltador-de-toros-minoico/titulo.texto: Minoan Bull-Leaper of the British Museum

fuentes/saltador-de-toros-minoico/resume.texto: Bronze group of a bull and a leaper, the only nearly complete three-dimensional sculptural group showing the Minoan bull leap. Evans dated it to Late Minoan IA, around 1600 BC; the leap it shows would be practically impossible, and it is thought to be a ritual representation.

fuentes/saltador-de-toros-minoico/por_qu.texto: It is used as evidence for the practice of bull-leaping, which the frescoes of Knossos also show.

fuentes/diosa-de-las-amapolas/resumen.texto: Female terracotta figurine of a large type of Minoan sculpture, found in 1937 in a sanctuary at Gazi, in Crete, and dated to the post-palatial period (Late Minoan III, 1400–1100 BC). It was probably a votive offering and not a cult image.

fuentes/diosa-de-las-amapolas/por_que_im.texto: It is an example of the large female terracotta figures of Late Minoan III.

fuentes/anillo-de-teseo/resumen.texto: Gold signet ring measuring 2.7 by 1.8 cm, from the 15th century BC, of Mycenaean date but with a theme typical of Minoan art: a scene of bull-leaping with a lion. It was found in the Anafiotika area of Athens; it was rejected as false, and in 2006 it was recognized as authentic.

fuentes/anillo-de-teseo/por_que_importa.texto: It is kept in the National Archaeological Museum of Athens.

fuentes/sarcofago-minoico-de-hannover/re.texto: Larnax, a ceramic coffin, from the 14th century BC (Late Minoan IIIA), probably from Crete, which entered the August Kestner Museum in Hannover in 1989. Larnakes were a common element of Late Minoan burials.

fuentes/sarcofago-minoico-de-hannover/po.texto: It shows the technique of Late Minoan painting, rougher than that of the palaces.

fuentes/kouros-de-palaikastro/resumen.texto: Gold and ivory statuette of a young man, about 50 cm tall, found in pieces at Palaikastro and dated to Late Minoan IB, in the mid-15th century BC. Because of its size and material it may have been a cult image, the only one known from Minoan civilization.

fuentes/kouros-de-palaikastro/por_que_im.texto: It is thought to represent the "young god" of late Minoan religion, son or companion of the great goddess.

fuentes/moldes-minoicos-de-palaikastro/r.texto: Two schist pieces with engraved faces, 225 by 100 mm, made as molds for casting plaques with figures and symbols, among them women with arms raised and double axes. They were found in 1899 near Palaikastro and published by Xanthoudides in 1900.

fuentes/moldes-minoicos-de-palaikastro/p.texto: They attest to the making of votive plaques with the double-axe, or labrys, symbol.

fuentes/fresco-del-boxeador-de-akrotiri/.texto: Fresco of the Boxing Boys of Akrotiri
Fresco found in 1967 at Akrotiri, showing two young men with boxing gloves and belts. It is dated to around 1700 BC, and the parts that are preserved intact were restored.
It is one of the main examples of Minoan painting and of the wall paintings of Thera.

fuentes/pinturas-murales-de-tera/resumen.texto: Set of frescoes discovered by Marinatos in the excavations of Akrotiri, on Santorini, from 1967 to 1974. They are considered part of Minoan art, although the culture of Thera was somewhat different from the Cretan one, and they were found more complete, and still on their walls, than those of Knossos.

fuentes/pinturas-murales-de-tera/por_que.texto: They give a view of the Bronze Age Aegean and of the culture of the island, and they were preserved under the cover of the eruption.

fuentes/fresco-de-la-tauromaquia-de-cnos.texto: Panels of painted relief stucco, the most restored of which shows a bull leap, which decorated the upper part of the east wall of the palace of Knossos. Its fragments fell during the destruction of the palace, probably in an earthquake, in Late Minoan II.
It shows the bull leap, a theme that also appears on other Minoan objects.

fuentes/la-parisienne/resumen.texto: Fragment of the fresco of the stools from the palace of Knossos, from the final phase of the palace (c. 1450–1350/1300 BC), excavated by Evans in 1901. Critics argue that it was retouched excessively by the restorers, among them Gilliéron.

fuentes/la-parisienne/por_que_importa.texto: It is a well-known image of Minoan painting and of the debate over Evans's restoration.

fuentes/copa-de-nestor-de-micenas/resume.texto: Gold cup 14.5 cm high and weighing about 296 g, which Schliemann found in 1876 in Shaft Grave IV of Grave Circle A at Mycenae, generally dated to the 16th century BC. It is in the National Archaeological Museum of Athens, and its name alludes to the cup of Nestor in the Iliad, from which it is separated by centuries.

fuentes/copa-de-nestor-de-micenas/por_qu.texto: It is one of the best-known pieces from the shaft graves.

fuentes/rhyton-de-plata-del-asedio/resum.texto: Silver vessel found in Shaft Grave IV of Grave Circle A at Mycenae, dated to around 1600–1500 BC (Late Helladic I), and named for its relief of an attack on a fortified city. It was probably used to carry the libations of sacred rituals.

fuentes/rhyton-de-plata-del-asedio/por_q.texto: Its relief shows a siege, a theme that is rare in Aegean art of the period.

fuentes/mascaras-funerarias-de-micenas/r.texto: Series of seven gold funerary masks found by Schliemann in 1876 in Grave Circle A at Mycenae, with the burials of six adult men and a child; no woman wore a mask. The best known is the so-called Mask of Agamemnon.

fuentes/mascaras-funerarias-de-micenas/p.texto: They are the most remarkable group from the shaft graves of Mycenae.

fuentes/estelas-funerarias-del-circulo-a.texto: Funerary stelae of Grave Circle A at Mycenae

At least 21 stelae found among the six shaft graves of Grave Circle A at Mycenae, of which twelve have identifiable reliefs; they are limestone slabs dated between 1600 and 1500 BC that marked the burials. They are similar to those of Grave Circle B and different from what the Minoans did.
They show how the shaft graves of Mycenae were marked in the 16th century BC.

fuentes/guijarro-de-kafkania/resumen.texto: River pebble about 5 cm long with marks that look like Linear B and a double axe, found on 1 April 1994 at Kafkania, 7 km north of Olympia, in a 17th-century BC context. If genuine, it would be the oldest writing on mainland Greece and by far the oldest document in Linear B; its authenticity and its reading are disputed, and Owens proposes that its origin is Minoan.

fuentes/guijarro-de-kafkania/por_que_imp.texto: If genuine, it would move writing on the mainland back more than two centuries.

fuentes/anfora-del-pulpo-de-prosimna/res.texto: Palatial three-handled amphora of the 15th century BC, found in the second tomb of the Mycenaean cemetery at Prosymna, near Argos. It is attributed to a Mycenaean painter working within the tradition of the marine style of Minoan Cretan pottery.

fuentes/anfora-del-pulpo-de-prosimna/por.texto: It shows how Mycenaean pottery inherited the Minoan repertoire in Late Helladic II.

fuentes/sartenes-cicladicas/resumen.texto: Flat discs with a «handle», of pottery and sometimes of stone, made in the Cyclades between c. 2700 and c. 2200 BC (Early Cycladic II); about 200 are known. A 2009 study showed experimentally that when filled with water or oil they served as mirrors.

fuentes/sartenes-cicladicas/por_que_impo.texto: They are a characteristic object of the Grotta-Pelos and Keros-Syros cultures, whose function is disputed.

fuentes/oxford-handbook-bronze-age-aegea.texto: The Oxford Handbook of the Bronze Age Aegean
Collective work edited by Eric H. Cline
Collective synthesis edited by Eric H. Cline, with chapters by specialists on the regions, architecture and trade of the Aegean between c. 3000 and c. 1000 BC.
It is a synthesis reference, later than the works of Evans, Furumark and Hood, which underpins the entries on sites and finds of more recent date.

fuentes/tesoro-de-egina/resumen.texto: Set of Minoan gold jewelry said to have been found on the island of Aegina, held by the British Museum since 1892. On the basis of its style and iconography it is dated between 1850 and 1550 BC, in Middle Minoan II and III. It includes earrings, diadems, a breast pendant, a bracelet, a gold cup and rings, along with beads of gold, lapis lazuli, amethyst, quartz, carnelian and jasper.

fuentes/tesoro-de-egina/por_que_importa.texto: It is among the most important ensembles of Minoan jewelry.

fuentes/colgante-de-las-abejas-de-malia/.texto: Gold pendant found in 1930 in a tomb at Chrysolakkos, in Malia, and first described by Pierre Demargne. It belongs to the protopalatial period and shows two identical insects, facing each other by the head, holding a central disc, with three discs hanging from the wings. It is in the Heraklion Archaeological Museum.
It is probably the most famous piece of Minoan jewelry.

fuentes/estructura-circular-de-papoura-f.texto: Architectural complex of concentric circles some 48 m in diameter on the summit of Papoura Hill, in Crete, found in 2024. It was used mainly between 2000 and 1700 BC and, judging by the Neopalatial pottery of the destruction layer, remained in use in later periods.
Its plan has no close parallel among the buildings of Crete from the same period.

fuentes/tablilla-en-lineal-b-de-iklaina/.texto: Fragment of a Linear B tablet found at Iklaina, in Messenia, with writing on both sides, from Late Helladic IIB–IIIA1 (1450–1350 BC).
It is the oldest Linear B tablet found so far on mainland Greece.

personas/schliemann/resumen.texto: German archaeologist who excavated Troy, Mycenae and Tiryns. At Mycenae he opened in 1876 the shaft graves of Grave Circle A, which he attributed to Agamemnon and his family; later dating places them in Late Helladic I, centuries before the time of the Trojan War.

personas/sofia-schliemann/resumen.texto: Greek, wife of Schliemann, who collaborated in his excavations of Troy and Mycenae. She appears beside him in the presentation of the jewels found at Troy and in the Mycenae tombs.

personas/evans/resumen.texto: British archaeologist who excavated the palace of Knossos from 1900 and named the Cretan civilization "Minoan". His Minoan chronology (Early, Middle and Late Minoan) is still in use, and his reconstructions of the palace, made with concrete, are disputed.

personas/kalokairinos/resumen.texto: Cretan merchant and antiquities dealer who excavated part of the palace of Knossos in 1878, on the hill of Kefala. His work preceded that of Evans.

personas/blegen/resumen.texto: American archaeologist. He excavated Troy, Zygouries, Prosymna and Pylos, where in 1939 he found the palace of Nestor with its Linear B tablets.

personas/marinatos/resumen.texto: Greek archaeologist who from 1967 excavated Akrotiri, on Santorini, where he found a Bronze Age city buried by the Minoan eruption. He proposed that the eruption ended Minoan civilization, a hypothesis that later dating does not support.

personas/ventris/resumen.texto: British architect who in 1952 showed that Linear B, the script of the tablets from Knossos and Pylos, transcribes an early form of Greek. He died in a road accident in 1956.

personas/chadwick/resumen.texto: British philologist who worked with Ventris on the decipherment of Linear B and co-signed with him Documents in Mycenaean Greek, of 1956.

personas/kober/resumen.texto: American linguist who, before Ventris, studied the inflections of Linear B and showed that the script records an inflected language. She died in 1950, before the decipherment.

personas/bennett/resumen.texto: American epigraphist who ordered the signs of Linear B and in 1951 published The Pylos Tablets, with the edition of the tablets from Pylos.

personas/tsountas/resumen.texto: Greek archaeologist, considered the first Greek prehistorian, who made the first formal excavations of the citadel of Mycenae, excavated Mycenaean tholos tombs in Laconia, such as the tholos of Vapheio, and gave the name to the Cycladic culture from his finds of the late 1890s.

personas/pernier/resumen.texto: Italian archaeologist who from 1900 directed the excavations of the Italian mission at Phaistos, where the Phaistos Disc was found in 1908.

personas/halbherr/resumen.texto: Italian archaeologist who explored Crete from 1884 and founded the Italian mission that excavated Phaistos and Agia Triada.

personas/boyd-hawes/resumen.texto: American archaeologist, discoverer and first director of the excavations at Gournia, one of the first Minoan settlements excavated on Crete.

personas/nikolaos-platon/resumen.texto: Greek archaeologist who discovered the Minoan palace of Zakros. Alongside Evans's chronology, based on pottery, he proposed a chronology of Crete by palatial periods (prepalatial, protopalatial, neopalatial and post-palatial).

personas/doerpfeld/resumen.texto: German architect and archaeologist, Schliemann's collaborator, who excavated Troy and Tiryns with him and recognized the phases of the palace of Tiryns.

personas/wace/resumen.texto: British archaeologist who excavated Mycenae between 1920 and 1955 and defined the sequence of Helladic pottery. In 1952 he also found Linear B tablets at Mycenae.

personas/pendlebury/resumen.texto: British archaeologist, curator at Knossos, who excavated in Crete and wrote a guide to Minoan archaeology. He died in Crete during the German invasion of 1941.

personas/hood/resumen.texto: British archaeologist, director of the British School at Athens from 1954 to 1962, who led the excavations at Knossos between 1957 and 1961 and wrote The Arts in Prehistoric Greece, a handbook of Aegean art.

personas/stamatakis/resumen.texto: Greek archaeologist, an official of the Archaeological Society at Athens, who represented the Greek government and the Society at Schliemann's excavations at Mycenae in 1876 and recorded and preserved the finds.

personas/mylonas/resumen.texto: Greek-American archaeologist who from 1952 excavated the Grave Circle B at Mycenae and other buildings of the citadel.

personas/papadimitriou/resumen.texto: Greek archaeologist who, with Mylonas, excavated the Grave Circle B at Mycenae, found in 1951, the oldest known monumental burial complex on the site.

personas/persson/resumen.texto: Swedish archaeologist, professor at Uppsala, who excavated Asine, Dendra and Midea in the Argolid. In 1926 he excavated a tholos tomb at Dendra.

personas/furumark/resumen.texto: Swedish archaeologist, specialist in the pottery of mainland Mycenaean Greece. His work The Mycenaean Pottery set a classification and a chronology of Late Bronze Age pottery of mainland Greece that is still used, with criticism of its rigidity.

personas/palmer/resumen.texto: British philologist, professor of comparative philology at Oxford from 1952 to 1971, who studied the language and dating of the Mycenaean Linear B tablets.

personas/minos/resumen.texto: King of Crete in Greek tradition, son of Zeus and Europa, to whom Thucydides attributes the first navy and dominion of the sea. He is a figure of mythology with no contemporary attestation: Evans took the name Minoan from this tradition.

personas/agamenon/resumen.texto: King of Mycenae and leader of the Greeks in the Iliad. A figure of epic and mythology, with no contemporary attestation; Hittite texts speak of a king of Ahhiyawa, but his name cannot be identified.

personas/nestor/resumen.texto: King of Pylos and counselor of the Achaeans in the Iliad. An epic figure with no contemporary attestation: the palace of Ano Englianos, excavated by Blegen, received his name through the Homeric tradition.

personas/atreo/resumen.texto: King of Mycenae, father of Agamemnon and Menelaus in Greek tradition. With no contemporary attestation; the so-called Treasury of Atreus, a tholos tomb at Mycenae, took its name from the tradition.

personas/teseo/resumen.texto: Athenian hero of Greek tradition who, according to myth, killed the Minotaur in the labyrinth of Knossos. A mythical figure: archaeology does not support the story, although Knossos was a great center of power.

personas/cadmo/resumen.texto: Mythical hero who, according to Greek tradition, founded the acropolis of Thebes, called the Cadmea. Archaeology shows Mycenaean occupation on the Cadmea, but there is no record of the figure.

personas/lamb/resumen.texto: British archaeologist, curator of Greek antiquities at the Fitzwilliam Museum in Cambridge from 1920 to 1958. In 1922 she excavated the tomb of Aegisthus at Mycenae, in the project led by Wace.

personas/sakellarakis/resumen.texto: Greek archaeologist specializing in Minoan prehistory, who in 1979 first excavated the temple of Anemospilia, on Crete. He interpreted the finds in the west room as a human sacrifice, a reading that others dispute.

personas/levi/resumen.texto: Italian archaeologist who conducted excavations in Italy, Greece and Turkey and directed the Italian mission at Phaistos and Agia Triada. He published Festos e la civiltà minoica.

personas/doumas/resumen.texto: Greek archaeologist, professor at the University of Athens, who was curator of antiquities in Attica, the Cyclades, the Dodecanese and the northern Aegean, and led excavations in those regions. Since 1975 he has directed the excavations at Akrotiri, as Marinatos's successor.

personas/throckmorton/resumen.texto: American photojournalist and pioneer of underwater archaeology, who in 1960 promoted and co-directed the excavation of the Bronze Age shipwreck at Cape Gelidonya, with the support of the University of Pennsylvania.

personas/du-plat-taylor/resumen.texto: British archaeologist, a pioneer of underwater archaeology, who co-directed with Throckmorton and Bass the excavation of the Cape Gelidonya shipwreck.

personas/bent/resumen.texto: English explorer and archaeologist who excavated in the Cyclades in the 1880s, before the work of Tsountas.

personas/mcdonald/resumen.texto: Canadian archaeologist who, in Blegen's first excavations at the palace of Nestor, unearthed the first Linear B tablets found on mainland Greece. From 1953 he carried out surveys in Messenia and directed the University of Minnesota Messenia Expedition (1961–1975).

personas/mackenzie/resumen.texto: Scottish archaeologist who assisted Arthur Evans in his excavations of the Minoan palace of Knossos. He was field supervisor of the British School at Athens' excavation of Phylakopi.

personas/gilleron/resumen.texto: Swiss artist and archaeological illustrator known for his reconstructions of Minoan and Mycenaean Bronze Age objects. His restorations of the Knossos frescoes, such as that of La Parisienne, were criticized for the changes he introduced.

personas/sackett/resumen.texto: British archaeologist, one of the discoverers of the kouros of Palaikastro. He co-directed with Mervyn Popham the excavations of Lefkandi and worked at Palaikastro.

personas/popham/resumen.texto: British archaeologist who in 1961 joined Sinclair Hood's team at Knossos, in 1962 excavated at Palaikastro with Hugh Sackett, and in 1964 began excavating Lefkandi-Xeropolis.

personas/hall-dohan/resumen.texto: American archaeologist, the first woman to earn a doctorate in classical archaeology at Bryn Mawr College. In 1904 she joined Harriet Boyd at Gournia and in 1910–1912 excavated Vrokastro.

personas/myres/resumen.texto: British archaeologist who in 1903 carried out at Petsofa the first systematic excavation of a Cretan peak sanctuary.

personas/bosanquet/resumen.texto: British archaeologist who, with Richard Dawkins, excavated the Minoan city of Roussolakkos, at Palaikastro, from 1902 to 1906. He was the first professor of classical archaeology at the University of Liverpool.

personas/dawkins/resumen.texto: British archaeologist and scholar of modern Greek who, with Robert Bosanquet, excavated the Minoan city of Roussolakkos, at Palaikastro, from 1902 to 1906.

personas/warren/resumen.texto: British archaeologist specializing in the Aegean Bronze Age, professor at the University of Bristol from 1977 to 2001. From 1967 to 1968 he directed the excavation of Fournou Korifi, at Myrtos, and published its report in 1972.

personas/stocker/resumen.texto: American archaeologist who, with her husband, directed the team that in 2015 found the intact tomb of the Griffin Warrior near the palace of Nestor.

personas/enkhelyawon/resumen.texto: Man of the 13th century BC known from the Linear B tablets of Pylos, which show him with large estates, a thousand vines and a thousand fig trees, and forty men as oarsmen of the fleet. He is assumed to have been the wanax of Pylos, but the tablets name the kings only by their title, and this cannot be proven.

personas/eritha/resumen.texto: Mycenaean priestess of Pylos who appears around 1180 BC in the Linear B tablets, in the cult of Sphagianes. In the last year of the palace she had a legal dispute with the damos over the status of her lands, the longest sentence preserved in Mycenaean Greek.

personas/bass/resumen.texto: American archaeologist, a pioneer of underwater archaeology. He directed the excavation of the Cape Gelidonya shipwreck, in 1960, and that of the Uluburun shipwreck.

hechos/cultura-cicladica-antigua/resumen.texto: The Early Cycladic culture developed in three phases between c. 3100 and 2300 BC in the Cyclades, with its marble figurines, pottery and cemeteries. The name "Cycladic" was established by Tsountas after his excavations of 1898–1899.

hechos/cultura-de-keros-siros/resumen.texto: The Keros-Syros culture corresponds to Early Cycladic II, c. 2700–2300 BC. It takes its name from the islands of Keros and Syros, and its best-preserved sites are also on Keos and Ios.

hechos/deposito-ritual-de-keros/titulo.texto: Deposit of broken figurines from Keros

hechos/deposito-ritual-de-keros/resumen.texto: At Kavos, on the west coast of Keros, figurines, vessels and marble objects were deposited broken before being buried. Renfrew's excavations of 2006–2008 date these activities to between 2750 and 2300 BC. The objects were broken elsewhere and brought to Kavos from various places of origin.

hechos/necropolis-de-jalandriani/resumen.texto: At Jalandriani, on Syros, more than 600 small tombs were used for burial during Early Cycladic II, with grave goods suggesting some social differentiation. Among the objects are "frying pans" decorated with rowing boats.

hechos/estructura-monumental-de-daskalio.texto: On the islet of Daskalio, opposite Kavos, a monumental stone structure was built in Early Cycladic II. It is linked to the ritual activity of the Keros deposit.

hechos/primer-asentamiento-de-filakopi/r.texto: Phylakopi, on the north coast of Melos, began in the middle of the 3rd millennium BC and was occupied until the 12th century BC. Its phases are the model for the chronology of the Cyclades, with a first town of the Early Cycladic period and a second of the Middle Cycladic period.

hechos/megaron-micenico-de-filakopi/resu.texto: In the upper layer of Phylakopi, in Late Helladic IIIA, a megaron of Mycenaean plan was built, with a central hall with a hearth and an antechamber, over a mansion of Late Bronze Age I. Mackenzie identified it in 1899 as a Mycenaean palace.

hechos/casa-de-las-tejas-de-lerna/titulo.texto: House of the Tiles at Lerna

hechos/casa-de-las-tejas-de-lerna/resume.texto: The House of the Tiles at Lerna is a monumental building of Early Helladic II, c. 2500–2300 BC, with a roof of clay tiles. It belongs to the phase called Lerna III, in which the Neolithic mound was leveled to build a new settlement.

hechos/poblado-de-poliojni/resumen.texto: Poliochni, on the east coast of Lemnos, is considered one of the oldest towns in Europe, older than Troy I. Its houses share party walls, and its decline is placed around 2000 BC; a commercial rivalry with Troy is assumed.

hechos/aparicion-de-los-jeroglificos-cre.texto: Around 2000 BC, in the period of the first palaces, a distinct hieroglyphic script appears in Crete, used mainly on seals and in clay. It is undeciphered and was abandoned in favor of Linear A.

hechos/primer-palacio-de-cnosos/resumen.texto: Around 1900 BC the first palace of Knossos was built on the hill of Kefala, serving for administration, storage and ritual; its seals and storage suggest a developed bureaucracy. Whether it was a royal residence is debated.

hechos/primeros-palacios-minoicos/titulo.texto: First palaces of Phaistos and Malia

hechos/primeros-palacios-minoicos/resume.texto: The palaces of Knossos, Phaistos and Malia were built in the protopalatial period, around 1900 BC. Five palaces on Crete are usually counted: Knossos, Phaistos, Malia, Galatas and Zakros.

hechos/aparicion-del-lineal-a/resumen.texto: Linear A was used in Crete from c. 1800 to c. 1450 BC on tablets, vessels and cult objects. It replaced the Cretan hieroglyphs in the period of the second palaces and has not been deciphered.

hechos/santuarios-de-altura-minoicos/res.texto: From the protopalatial period the summits of Cretan mountains, such as Juktas, were used as sanctuaries, with offerings of clay figurines. They are cult sites without a temple, dependent on the nearby palaces.

hechos/cuevas-sagradas-minoicas/resumen.texto: Caves such as Arkalochori, used from the 3rd millennium until c. 1450 BC, and Psychro held Minoan votive offerings, including axes and figurines.

hechos/disco-de-festos-depositado/resume.texto: The Phaistos Disc, of baked clay with signs stamped in a spiral, was deposited around 1700 BC in a palace building, where the Italian mission found it in 1908. It is not known what language it transcribes.

hechos/destruccion-de-los-primeros-palac.texto: Destruction of the first Minoan palaces

Around 1700 BC the first palace of Knossos and other centers of Crete were destroyed, probably by earthquakes, although a violent destruction has been proposed. The palaces were rebuilt larger and with richer decoration.

hechos/anemospilia-destruccion/resumen.texto: The temple of Anemospilia, on the slope of Juktas, was destroyed by an earthquake and fire around 1700 BC. In the west room the skeletons of a woman and a man were found, and another body with a knife. Sakellarakis read it as a human sacrifice; others, such as Hughes, say the knife was a fallen spearhead and that there is no evidence of an altar.

hechos/segundo-palacio-de-cnosos/resumen.texto: The palace of Knossos was rebuilt after 1700 BC with a central courtyard, staircases, storerooms, reception halls, light wells, drains and frescoes. It was the height of its power and that of the city around it, which by one estimate had some 30,000 inhabitants around 1360 BC.

hechos/palacio-de-galatas/resumen.texto: On a settlement of Middle Minoan IB, the palace of Galatas was built around 1750 BC; it was destroyed by fire at the end of Middle Minoan IIIA.

hechos/palacio-de-zakros/resumen.texto: The palace of Zakros, on the east coast of Crete, was built around 1900 BC and rebuilt around 1600 BC. It was a center of trade with the east; Platon excavated it from 1961.

hechos/destruccion-del-palacio-de-zakros.texto: Destruction of the palace of Zakros
The palace of Zakros was destroyed around 1450 BC, in the same period as the other major Minoan centers.

hechos/erupcion-minoica/resumen.texto: The eruption of Thera, with an explosivity index of 7, covered the settlement of Akrotiri with pumice and ash and affected the coasts of Crete. The date is disputed: radiocarbon places it around 1600 BC or earlier, while traditional archaeology, synchronizing Minoan pottery with Egypt, places it around 1500 BC; a 2018 recalibration brings both dates together in the 16th century BC.

hechos/abandono-de-akrotiri/resumen.texto: The city of Akrotiri was buried under a layer of pumice and ash from the Minoan eruption and was preserved until Marinatos excavated it from 1967. There are signs that its inhabitants returned to recover their belongings.

hechos/tsunamis-en-la-costa-norte-de-cre.texto: Tsunamis of the Minoan eruption on Crete
The Minoan eruption caused waves on the north coast of Crete that reached Amnisos, where they knocked walls out of alignment, and Palaikastro. In the northeast, earthquakes destroyed Petras.

hechos/fin-de-los-palacios-minoicos/resu.texto: Destructions across Crete around 1470–1450 BC, which seem deliberate because they spared some sites (at Knossos the town burned but not the palace), ended Neopalatial society. The palace of Knossos remained in use under the Mycenaeans. Their causes are debated.

hechos/micenizacion-de-cnosos/resumen.texto: After c. 1450 BC Knossos functioned as an administrative center of Mycenaean Greeks: the Linear B tablets record lands, labor, flocks and textiles. How and when control passed into Mycenaean hands is debated.

hechos/adopcion-del-lineal-b/resumen.texto: After 1450 BC a modified version of Linear A was used at Knossos to write Mycenaean Greek, which came to be called Linear B. The date of the Knossos tablets is debated between c. 1400 and c. 1200 BC.

hechos/destruccion-del-palacio-de-cnosos.texto: Destruction of the palace of Knossos

A fire destroyed the palace of Knossos, conventionally dated to around 1350 BC; the date of the final destruction and the meaning of the later materials are still under study. Palmer placed it in the 13th century BC.

hechos/tumba-del-guerrero-del-grifo/resu.texto: A shaft grave of c. 1450 BC near the palace of Nestor held a warrior and more than 3,500 objects, including weapons, jewelry, silver and gold, the agate of the combat and four gold rings with scenes from Minoan mythology. It was excavated in 2015.

hechos/tumbas-de-fosa-del-circulo-b/titu.texto: Shaft graves of Grave Circle B at Mycenae

hechos/tumbas-de-fosa-del-circulo-b/resu.texto: Grave Circle B, outside the walls, is a cemetery of cist graves of the Middle Helladic period and of deeper shaft graves, with rich grave goods and stelae. It is older than Grave Circle A.

hechos/tumbas-de-fosa-del-circulo-a/titu.texto: Shaft graves of Grave Circle A at Mycenae

hechos/tumbas-de-fosa-del-circulo-a/resu.texto: Six shaft graves inside the citadel, with 19 burials, among them men with swords, daggers and gold masks, show a warrior elite in Late Helladic I. Schliemann attributed them to Agamemnon, but they are about three centuries earlier than the time of the epic.

hechos/autenticidad-de-la-mascara-de-aga.texto: Debate over the authenticity of the Mask of Agamemnon

The gold mask from Shaft Grave V of Grave Circle A is dated to the 16th century BC. At the end of the 20th and beginning of the 21st century William M. Calder III and David Traill questioned its authenticity and proposed that Schliemann had it made by a forger; other specialists defend it as ancient.

hechos/influencia-minoica-en-la-grecia-c.texto: From c. 1600 BC the shaft graves of Mycenae and finds such as the Vapheio cups show a strong Cretan influence, both through imports and through workshops on mainland Greece.

hechos/tholoi-micenicos/resumen.texto: After the first tholoi of Mycenae, from Late Helladic IIB the Mycenaean elites built tholos tombs: Wace grouped them in three series, from Kato Phournos and Panagia to the Treasury of Atreus. They replaced shaft graves.

hechos/tesoro-de-atreo-construccion/titu.texto: Construction of the Treasury of Atreus

hechos/tesoro-de-atreo-construccion/resu.texto: Between 1300 and 1250 BC the largest known tholos of the Aegean was built at Mycenae, with a corbelled dome that was the largest in the world until the Roman period. Its name is modern: Pausanias describes it without associating it with Atreus.

hechos/murallas-ciclopeas-de-micenas/res.texto: Around 1350 BC the fortifications of the Mycenae acropolis were rebuilt in cyclopean masonry, so called because blocks so large were later attributed to the Cyclopes.

hechos/puerta-de-los-leones-construccion.texto: In the middle of Late Helladic IIIB, around 1250 BC, the wall of Mycenae was extended along the west slope to include Grave Circle A, and the main entrance, the Lion Gate, was made.

hechos/murallas-y-palacio-de-tirinto/res.texto: The acropolis of Tiryns was built in three phases, from the end of Late Helladic II to the end of IIIB, with cyclopean walls and a palace with a megaron. Around 1300 BC it had some 10,000 inhabitants.

hechos/destruccion-del-palacio-de-tirint.texto: Destruction of the palace of Tiryns
The palace of Tiryns was destroyed around 1200 BC; despite this, the city's population kept growing, to some 15,000 inhabitants around 1150 BC.

hechos/palacio-de-nestor-hecho/titulo.texto: Palace of Nestor at Ano Englianos

hechos/palacio-de-nestor-hecho/resumen.texto: The palace of Ano Englianos, in Messenia, is the center of the Mycenaean kingdom of Pylos, which according to the tablets covered some 2,000 km². Most of the objects found date from after 1300 BC.

hechos/destruccion-del-palacio-de-nestor.texto: Destruction of the palace of Pylos

A fire destroyed the palace of Pylos, dated to c. 1200–1180 BC (end of Late Helladic IIIB), and baked the Linear B tablets that were preserved; the tablets mention preparations for defense against an attack without saying who was attacking.

hechos/reino-de-pilos-segun-el-lineal-b/.texto: Kingdom of Pylos according to Linear B
The Pylos tablets show a kingdom with centralized administration, divided into provinces, controlling bronze, livestock and textiles. They give the names of gods and officials.

hechos/destruccion-del-palacio-de-tebas/.texto: Destruction of the palace of Thebes
The palace buildings of the Cadmea were destroyed by fire at the end of Late Helladic IIIB; the city declined and much of the site was abandoned.

hechos/destruccion-de-micenas-hacia-1190.texto: A destruction of buildings in the Mycenae citadel around 1190 BC, in the collapse of c. 1200, ended its role as a great power; it remained inhabited, partly rebuilt, without palace administration. Another later fire, which one synthesis dates to around 1150 BC, was the last: afterwards it was sparsely inhabited until the Hellenistic period.

hechos/gla-construccion/resumen.texto: Gla, on an island in Lake Copais, is the largest Mycenaean fortress in Boeotia: its cyclopean walls, 2.8 km long, enclose some 20 hectares, ten times more than Athens or Tiryns, with four gates. It is debated whether it was a palace or a military center with storerooms.

hechos/acropolis-de-atenas-micenica/titu.texto: Palace and cyclopean wall of the Acropolis

hechos/acropolis-de-atenas-micenica/resu.texto: In the Late Bronze Age a megaron palace was built on the Acropolis and, shortly afterwards, a cyclopean wall 760 m long. Almost nothing of the palace survives.

hechos/tholos-de-orcomeno/resumen.texto: Orchomenos in Boeotia had a tholos tomb in the Late Bronze Age, which Pausanias recalls as the treasury of the Minyans.

hechos/tumba-de-vafio/resumen.texto: The tomb of Vapheio, in Laconia, has a corridor about 30 m long and a chamber 10 m in diameter; its gold cups are attributed to Minoan or mainland workshops.

hechos/panoplia-de-dendra-hecho/resumen.texto: In a chamber tomb at Dendra, at the end of the 15th century BC, a fifteen-piece bronze armor was buried; it is the oldest known beaten-bronze cuirass.

hechos/cartas-de-los-ahhiyawa-y-grecia-m.texto: Identification of Ahhiyawa with the Mycenaeans
Hittite texts mention a power called Ahhiyawa, which several specialists identify with the Mycenaeans of Greece; the name recalls Homer's Achaeans. The identification has not been proven.

hechos/millawanda-micenica/resumen.texto: Miletus had a Minoan presence from c. 1900 BC and in the Late Bronze Age was under Mycenaean influence; Hittite texts call it Millawanda.

hechos/micenicos-en-rodas/resumen.texto: The Minoans founded a settlement at Trianda, in northwest Rhodes, around the 16th century BC, and in the 15th century BC Mycenaean Greeks settled on the island.

hechos/micenicos-en-chipre/titulo.texto: Mycenaean pottery and trade in Cyprus

hechos/micenicos-en-chipre/resumen.texto: In the Late Bronze Age Mycenaean pottery arrives in quantity in Cyprus and at sites such as Enkomi, Hala Sultan Tekke and Kition, through the copper trade. After 1200 a population of Aegean origin settled there, according to some scholars.

hechos/naufragio-de-uluburun/resumen.texto: A ship about 15 m long, with more than 20 tons of cargo (copper and tin ingots, terebinth resin, pottery and glass), sank at the end of the 14th century BC south of Kaş, on the coast of Anatolia. It was found in 1982.

hechos/naufragio-de-cabo-gelidonya/resum.texto: A Late Bronze Age ship sank around 1200 BC at a depth of about 27 m off Cape Gelidonya, on the south coast of Anatolia. It was located in 1954 and has been excavated since 1960.

hechos/talasocracia-de-minos-tradicion/r.texto: Thucydides says that Minos had the first fleet and dominated the Aegean. No contemporary text supports this, and specialists debate whether Crete controlled the sea.

hechos/laberinto-y-minotauro-tradicion/t.texto: Tradition of the labyrinth and the Minotaur

hechos/laberinto-y-minotauro-tradicion/r.texto: Greek tradition says that Minos had a labyrinth built at Knossos for the Minotaur, which Theseus killed. It is a legend: archaeology shows only a large palace of complex plan. After the decipherment of Linear B a form was identified that reads da-pu₂-ri-to, taken as the Mycenaean version of "labyrinth".

hechos/tradicion-de-la-invasion-doria/re.texto: Greek tradition says that the Dorians, led by the Heraclidae, occupied the Peloponnese shortly after Troy. Today archaeology considers the hypothesis of an invasion discarded.

hechos/periodo-submicenico/resumen.texto: After Late Helladic IIIC, around 1100–1050 BC, sub-Mycenaean pottery spreads, marking the end of the Bronze Age in Greece; at Lefkandi, cemeteries document it.

hechos/refugios-minoicos-del-minoico-tar.texto: Refuge settlements of Late Minoan IIIC
In Late Minoan IIIC, around 1200–1075 BC, the population of Crete took refuge in high sites such as Karphi and Vrokastro.

hechos/lefkandi-heladico-tardio-iiic/res.texto: The settlement of Xeropolis, at Lefkandi, has strata of Late Helladic IIIC that allowed the pottery sequence of that period to be fixed, and a settlement that contrasts with that of other sites in Greece.

hechos/perati-cementerio/resumen.texto: The Perati necropolis, on the east coast of Attica, of Late Helladic IIIC, was used for a century and had imports from the Cyclades, the Dodecanese, Crete, Cyprus, Egypt and Syria.

hechos/desciframiento-del-lineal-b/resum.texto: In 1952 Ventris, with the earlier work of Kober and Bennett, showed that Linear B transcribes an early form of Greek, Mycenaean Greek. Chadwick accompanied him in the books that followed.

hechos/dioses-en-las-tablillas-micenicas.texto: The Linear B tablets name gods who later appear in the Greek pantheon: Poseidon, Zeus, Dionysus and Artemis, and a Potnia ("Lady") with her own sanctuary. Mycenaean religion is little known from the archaeological record.

hechos/wanax-y-lawagetas/resumen.texto: In the Pylos tablets the wanax, the sovereign, heads the state, and below him is a palace administration; another title, the lawagetas, is usually understood as a military leader. What each of them did exactly is debated.

hechos/palacios-micenicos-hacia-1400/res.texto: Around 1400 BC the true palaces of mainland Greece are dated: Mycenae and Tiryns, with cyclopean walls, and then Midea, Pylos, Athens, Eleusis, Thebes, Orchomenos and Iolcos, the northernmost Mycenaean center. From the beginning of the 14th century BC Mycenaean trade reached Cyprus, the Levant and Apulia, in the gap left by the Minoan collapse.

hechos/ceramica-de-kamares-hecho/resumen.texto: Between c. 2100 and 1450 BC Kamares ware, with light decoration on a dark ground, was produced in Crete. It was traded throughout the Aegean and reached the Levant and Egypt.

hechos/sellos-minoicos-hecho/resumen.texto: Minoan seals of stone and metal, found in quantity at Knossos, Malia and Phaistos, were used to mark documents and objects.

hechos/figurillas-cicladicas-de-brazos-c.texto: Marble figurines with folded arms, of which a large number is known, are the best-known expression of Cycladic art. Most were removed without a record of their context.

hechos/casco-de-colmillos-de-jabali-hech.texto: From the shaft graves of Mycenae to Elateia, in the 10th century BC, Aegean warriors wore leather helmets covered with boar's tusk plates.

hechos/exportaciones-de-vasijas-minoicas.texto: From the 18th century BC vessels containing oils and unguents were exported from Crete. They have been found in the Aegean, mainland Greece, Cyprus, the Syrian coast and Egypt, showing the trade contacts of the Minoans.

hechos/asentamientos-minoicos-en-el-egeo.texto: There were Minoan settlements outside Crete, at Kythera (Kastri), Akrotiri and Miletus, and it is debated whether they formed a political domain of Crete or networks of trade.

hechos/tumbas-de-tholos-de-la-mesara/res.texto: In the Mesara, in southern Crete, the prepalatial cemeteries of Kumasa, Apesokari and Kamilari have tholos tombs for collective use.

hechos/destruccion-de-monastiraki/resume.texto: The Minoan settlement of Monastiraki, on the Amari plain, was destroyed at the same time as the first palaces and was never reoccupied.

hechos/abandono-de-gurnia/resumen.texto: The settlement of Gournia, occupied from Early Minoan II, ceased to be inhabited at the end of Late Minoan IA, around 1470 BC, in the destructions that ended the Minoan palaces.

hechos/villa-real-de-agia-triada/resumen.texto: In the Neopalatial period the great royal villa was built at Agia Triada, next to Phaistos; the painted sarcophagus and the Harvester Vase came from its site.

hechos/archivo-de-lineal-a-de-agia-triad.texto: Linear A archive of Agia Triada
The largest set of Linear A tablets, some 150, was found at Agia Triada, along with 23 roundels and many sealed clay nodules. All are of Late Minoan IA.

hechos/tumba-de-egisto-construccion/resu.texto: Tholos tomb near the Mycenae citadel, from Late Helladic IIA, c. 1510–1450 BC, with features intermediate between the earliest tholoi and the later ones.

hechos/volimidia-cementerio/resumen.texto: A cemetery of 35 tombs, mostly chamber tombs, and a settlement occupied until c. 1180 BC, in the territory of the palace of Pylos.

hechos/drenaje-del-lago-copais/resumen.texto: A system of dikes and canals more than 50 km long drained Lake Copais around the time Gla was built, producing a fertile plain. The system broke down, through destruction or abandonment, at the end of Mycenaean civilization.

hechos/cultura-de-grotta-pelos/resumen.texto: The Grotta-Pelos culture is a cultural dating system of the Early Bronze Age, which marks the beginning of Cycladic culture and runs from the Late Neolithic (c. 3300 BC) to c. 2700 BC.

hechos/cultura-de-kastri/resumen.texto: Colin Renfrew called the Cycladic phase of c. 2500–2200 BC the Kastri culture, after the fortified settlement of Kastri, near Jalandriani, on Syros. The settlement, associated with the Jalandriani necropolis, was fortified and is cited as an example of the fortifications of Early Cycladic II.

hechos/cultura-de-filakopi-i/resumen.texto: Renfrew called the Cycladic phase of c. 2300–2000 BC the Phylakopi I culture, after the settlement of Phylakopi, on Melos.

hechos/cultura-de-eutresis/resumen.texto: The Eutresis culture, or Early Helladic I, was the initial phase of the Bronze Age on mainland Greece, c. 3200 to c. 2650 BC, and was followed by the Korakou culture.

hechos/cultura-de-korakou/resumen.texto: The Korakou culture, or Early Helladic II, lasted from c. 2650 to c. 2200 BC and followed the Eutresis culture; it was sometimes succeeded by a Lefkandi culture (Early Helladic IIB).

hechos/cultura-de-tirinto/resumen.texto: The Tiryns culture, or Early Helladic III (2200–2000 BC), was an Early Bronze Age culture of central and southern Greece and of the Ionian Islands, which followed the Eutresis and Korakou cultures and preceded Mycenaean civilization.

hechos/ceramica-minia/resumen.texto: Minyan ware is the burnished pottery of the Middle Helladic period (c. 2000/1900–1550 BC). Schliemann coined the term on finding it at Orchomenos, and the excavations of the 1960s showed that it evolved from the burnished pottery of the Tiryns culture.

hechos/ceramica-de-vasiliki/resumen.texto: Vasiliki ware is a type of Minoan pottery of Early Minoan II, with an uneven reddish slip that imitates stone vessels, named after the site of Vasiliki.

hechos/kouloures-minoicas/resumen.texto: The kouloures are circular underground pits with stone walls at the palaces of Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, built around Middle Minoan II (1850–1750 BC). Evans named them in 1903 for their resemblance to the Greek round bread, and their function is debated.

hechos/estructura-circular-de-papoura/re.texto: Architectural complex of concentric circles some 48 m in diameter, found in 2024 on the summit of Papoura Hill, in Crete. It was used mainly between 2000 and 1700 BC and, judging by the Neopalatial pottery of the destruction layer, remained in use in later periods.

hechos/sala-del-trono-de-cnosos/resumen.texto: The throne room, in the center of the palace of Knossos, was built in the 15th century BC, and Evans excavated it in 1900. It took its final form in Late Minoan IIIA, and several archaeologists maintain that its furnishings date from after 1450 BC, from the Mycenaean takeover of the palace.

hechos/estilo-palaciego-minoico/resumen.texto: Palace Style is a style of Minoan pottery, so named by Evans, which flourished in Late Minoan II (c. 1450–1400 BC). It disappears with the final destruction of the palace of Knossos around 1400 BC.

hechos/tumbas-de-camara-micenicas/resume.texto: Mycenaean chamber tombs, cut into the rock, appear in Messenia at the end of the Middle Helladic period (c. 1600 BC), and in Late Helladic I they are found in central and southern Greece, above all in the Argolid. They were used throughout the Late Bronze Age.

hechos/primeros-tholoi-de-micenas/resume.texto: The tholos tombs called the Cyclopean Tomb, Epano Phournos and Kato Phournos, at Mycenae, are among the earliest at the site and date from Late Helladic IIA (c. 1635/1600–1480/1470 BC). The one at Epano Phournos was used for a single burial.

hechos/destruccion-del-palacio-de-malia/.texto: Destruction of the palace of Malia
The palace of Malia, the third largest Minoan palace, was destroyed at the end of Late Minoan IB, around 1470–1450 BC.

hechos/destruccion-del-palacio-de-festos.texto: Destruction of the palace of Phaistos

The palace of Phaistos, whose first building was constructed in Middle Minoan IB (c. 2000 BC), was destroyed around 1450 BC with the other Minoan palaces, although some dates bring this down to c. 1400, and it was not rebuilt.

hechos/destruccion-del-palacio-de-galata.texto: Destruction of the palace of Galatas
A fire destroyed the palace center of Galatas at the end of Middle Minoan IIIA.

hechos/destruccion-de-agia-triada/titulo.texto: Destruction and abandonment of Agia Triada

hechos/destruccion-de-agia-triada/resume.texto: Agia Triada suffered a fire in Late Minoan I (c. 1625–1470 BC) and in the 13th century BC it was destroyed and abandoned; around 1050–900 BC a sanctuary was set up there.

hechos/palacio-de-agios-vasileios/resume.texto: The Mycenaean palace of Agios Vasileios, in Laconia, was built in Late Helladic IIIA (1400–1300 BC). The site grew to some 20 hectares. It has an archive of Linear B tablets, the first of which was found in 2008.

hechos/destruccion-del-palacio-de-agios-.texto: Destruction of the palace of Agios Vasileios
The palace of Agios Vasileios suffered a fire in Late Helladic IIIB (c. 1300–1200 BC), was partly rebuilt, and not long afterward was destroyed again.

hechos/destruccion-del-palacio-de-midea/.texto: The first megaron of the palace of Midea, built in Late Helladic IIIB2, was destroyed around 1200 BC along with the rest of the settlement.

hechos/presa-de-tirinto/resumen.texto: After a mudslide, perhaps caused by an earthquake, that buried part of Tiryns at the end of Late Helladic IIIB2, a dam about 10 m high and 300 m long was built to divert the Lakissa River. It is dated to the beginning of Late Helladic IIIC or, according to another dating, to around 1260 BC.

hechos/puente-de-arkadiko/resumen.texto: The Arkadiko Bridge, near the road from Tiryns to Epidaurus, is a corbelled arch bridge built in cyclopean style in Late Helladic III (c. 1300–1190 BC). It is one of the oldest arch bridges that can still be crossed.

hechos/fortificacion-de-teichos-dymaion/.texto: The acropolis of Teichos Dymaion, in western Peloponnese, was built in the Mycenaean period, probably around 1300 BC, on a site occupied since c. 3500 BC.

hechos/tablilla-de-iklaina/resumen.texto: At Iklaina, near Pylos, a fragment of a Linear B tablet with writing on both sides was found, from Late Helladic IIB–IIIA1 (1450–1350 BC).

hechos/disputa-legal-de-eritha/resumen.texto: In the last year before the destruction of the palace of Pylos, the priestess Eritha had a dispute with the damos of Sphagianes over the status of her lands, which she said were held in the name of her deity. The record is the longest sentence preserved in Mycenaean Greek and the earliest evidence of a legal dispute in Europe; how it ended is unknown, and Sphagianes may be identified with Volimidia.

hechos/keftiu-en-tumbas-de-funcionarios-.texto: The keftiu in the tombs of Theban officials

The reliefs in the tombs of Theban officials, from the reigns of Hatshepsut to Amenhotep II, among them those of Senenmut and of Rekhmire, the vizier, show the keftiu as bearers of gifts or tribute. The earliest representations are in the tomb of Senenmut. Keftiu is usually read as Crete or Cretan people, although the identification is debated.

hechos/lista-egea-de-amenhotep-iii/titul.texto: Aegean place-name list of Amenhotep III

hechos/lista-egea-de-amenhotep-iii/lugar.texto: Mortuary Temple of Amenhotep III (Kom el-Hettan)

hechos/lista-egea-de-amenhotep-iii/resum.texto: The list of Aegean place names of Amenhotep III includes, among the villages of Keftiu, Kenesch (Knossos), Byschty (Phaistos), Amnesch (Amnisos), Keteny (Kydonia) and Leket (Lyktos).

hechos/contactos-micenicos-con-italia-y-.texto: Mycenaean contacts with Italy and Sicily

Roca Vecchia, in Apulia, has the largest set of Mycenaean pottery found west of mainland Greece; at Vivara Mycenaean fragments were found next to Proto-Apennine and Apennine pottery from a Middle Bronze Age emporium, and at Thapsos, in Sicily, the historian David Abulafia sees a culture imported from a Mycenaean origin.

hechos/asentamiento-de-ayia-irini-en-ceo.texto: On Kea there was a Bronze Age settlement at the site now called Ayia Irini, which reached its height in the Late Minoan and Early Late Helladic periods, between 1600 and 1400 BC.

hechos/tumba-de-clitemnestra-construccio.texto: Construction of the Tomb of Clytemnestra
Tholos tomb at Mycenae built around 1250 BC, with a facade of half-columns of plaster and a dromos with ashlar walls. Its name comes from later tradition.

lugares/cnosos/resumen.texto: Largest center of Minoan civilization, on the hill of Kefala, near Heraklion. The first palace was built c. 1900 BC and, after a destruction c. 1700 BC, was rebuilt; the site was occupied from the Neolithic to the Roman period.

lugares/festos/resumen.texto: Minoan center of the Mesara plain, in southern Crete, with a palace and the city around it. The Phaistos Disc came from its ruins, and it is close to Agia Triada.

lugares/malia/resumen.texto: Minoan and Mycenaean site on the north coast of Crete, in the Heraklion area, occupied from the middle of the 3rd millennium BC to c. 1250 BC; in Late Minoan I it had the third largest Minoan palace, destroyed at the end of Late Minoan IB.

lugares/zakros/resumen.texto: Minoan site on the east coast of Crete, with a palace and a sheltered harbor for trade to the east. The palace was built around 1900 BC, rebuilt around 1600 BC and destroyed around 1450 BC.

lugares/galatas/resumen.texto: Minoan site in central Crete, southeast of Heraklion, discovered in the 1990s. A palace was built around 1750 BC on a protopalatial settlement, and it was destroyed by fire.

lugares/petras/resumen.texto: Minoan settlement in northeast Crete, with a building of features similar to the Minoan palaces, which is sometimes called a palace. It is considered inhabited until c. 1450 BC.

lugares/gurnia/resumen.texto: Minoan settlement of the Gulf of Mirabello, with a palatial core and paved streets. It was occupied from Early Minoan II to Late Minoan I.

lugares/agia-triada/resumen.texto: Minoan settlement of the Mesara, 3 km from Phaistos, with a large royal villa. It yielded a painted sarcophagus, the Harvester Vase and some 150 Linear A tablets, the largest such set.

lugares/kommos/resumen.texto: Minoan port on the south coast of Crete, near Phaistos and Agia Triada, with monumental buildings and evidence of trade with Cyprus, the Levant and Egypt.

lugares/mojlos/resumen.texto: Minoan island and settlement of the Gulf of Mirabello, in eastern Crete, which in Minoan times was joined to the land and served as an eastern port. It has tombs of the Early Minoan period.

lugares/vasiliki/resumen.texto: Minoan site on the Ierapetra isthmus, with a village occupied from Early Minoan IIA to Late Minoan IA.

lugares/arkalochori/resumen.texto: Minoan sacred cave of central Crete, used from the 3rd millennium BC to c. 1450 BC, when its roof collapsed and sealed votive offerings, among them the Arkalochori Axe.

lugares/palaikastro/resumen.texto: Large Minoan settlement at the eastern tip of Crete, with an urban sector at Roussolakkos, behind Chiona beach; the region was already a trade center in Minoan times.

lugares/arkanes/resumen.texto: Minoan settlement in central Crete, a junction of roads to Juktas, Anemospilia and Vathypetro, with a necropolis at Phourni.

lugares/zominthos/resumen.texto: Large Minoan building on a plateau of Mount Ida, on the road between Knossos and the Ida cave; there has been permanent occupation since c. 1800 BC.

lugares/tilisos/resumen.texto: Minoan site with three large villas, in central Crete, west of Heraklion, occupied since the Minoan period.

lugares/monastiraki/resumen.texto: Minoan settlement on the Amari plain, which was not reoccupied after its destruction around 1700 BC and is one of the best examples of Middle Minoan archaeology.

lugares/psira/resumen.texto: Minoan island in the Gulf of Mirabello, near Mochlos and Gournia, with a settlement from the Early to the Late Minoan period.

lugares/fournou-korifi/resumen.texto: Minoan settlement of Early Minoan II, on top of a hill near Myrtos, in southern Crete, with a group of attached rooms.

lugares/pirgos-de-mirtos/resumen.texto: Minoan settlement on the south coast of Crete, near Furnu Korifi, with a Middle Minoan building and a large Neopalatial villa. It was established around 3000 BC, destroyed by fire around 2150 BC and reoccupied around 1900 BC.

lugares/anemospilia/resumen.texto: Minoan temple of Middle Minoan III on the north slope of Mount Juktas, in Crete, destroyed by an earthquake around 1700 BC; the human remains are debated as a possible sacrifice.

lugares/juktas/resumen.texto: Minoan peak sanctuary on the summit of Mount Juktas, south of Knossos, in use since the protopalatial period.

lugares/cueva-de-psychro/resumen.texto: Cave of Dikte, on the Lasithi plateau, in eastern Crete, used as a sanctuary since Minoan times; later tradition associates it with the birth of Zeus.

lugares/kamares/resumen.texto: Mountain cave on the slope of Mount Ida, in the Mesara, which gave its name to Kamares ware of the Middle Minoan period.

lugares/kato-simi/resumen.texto: Minoan peak sanctuary in southern Crete, used since the protopalatial period.

lugares/amnisos/resumen.texto: Port of Knossos on the north coast of Crete; a tsunami from the Minoan eruption knocked its walls out of alignment.

lugares/cidonia/resumen.texto: Minoan settlement at the site of La Canea (Chania), on the northwest coast of Crete.

lugares/furni/resumen.texto: Minoan necropolis of Arkhanes, in central Crete, used for much of the Bronze Age.

lugares/crisolakos/resumen.texto: Protopalatial Minoan necropolis of Malia, with monumental tombs of the elite.

lugares/karfi/resumen.texto: Refuge settlement on the Lasithi plateau, in eastern Crete, of Late Minoan IIIC, in the mountains.

lugares/vrokastro/resumen.texto: Mountain settlement above the Gulf of Mirabello, in eastern Crete, with an initial Middle Minoan occupation, a reoccupation around 1250 BC and burials from c. 1200 to c. 700–650 BC; it was excavated by Edith Hall Dohan in 1910–1912.

lugares/kavusi/resumen.texto: Site on the Vronda ridge, above the Gulf of Mirabello, in eastern Crete, with a Dark Age village of Late Minoan IIIC (c. 1170–1050 BC) and an Early Iron Age cemetery.

lugares/keros/resumen.texto: Uninhabited island of the Cyclades, about 10 km southeast of Naxos, important for the Cycladic culture of c. 2500 BC, with a ritual deposit of broken figurines.

lugares/daskalio/resumen.texto: Islet next to Keros with a monumental marble structure of Early Cycladic II, which in the literature is associated with the cult of the broken figurines of the Kavos deposit.

lugares/jalandriani/resumen.texto: Largest known Early Cycladic necropolis, on Syros, with more than 600 tombs; it is linked to the fortified settlement of Kastri.

lugares/filakopi/resumen.texto: Settlement on Melos, on the north coast of the island, occupied from the middle of the 3rd millennium BC to the 12th century BC; it is the reference site for the chronology of the Cyclades.

lugares/akrotiri/resumen.texto: Bronze Age settlement in the south of Thera, buried by the Minoan eruption and excavated since 1967 by Marinatos; its houses keep frescoes on several floors.

lugares/skarkos/resumen.texto: Early Cycladic settlement on the island of Ios, from the middle of the 3rd millennium BC, with two-story buildings and four-meter walls, and a later cemetery of the Middle and Late Bronze Age.

lugares/markiani/resumen.texto: Fortified Early Cycladic settlement on the island of Amorgos.

lugares/kastri-de-citera/resumen.texto: Settlement on Kythera occupied since the Bronze Age, considered one of the first Minoan settlements outside Crete.

lugares/poliojni/resumen.texto: Settlement on the east coast of Lemnos, in the north Aegean, one of the oldest in Europe, excavated by the Italian mission since 1930.

lugares/emporio/resumen.texto: Settlement on the island of Chios with occupation from the Neolithic to the Bronze Age.

lugares/lerna/resumen.texto: Site in the Argolid, next to the gulf, famous for the House of the Tiles, a monumental building of Early Helladic II, c. 2500–2300 BC.

lugares/asine/resumen.texto: Settlement on the coast of the Argolid with continuous Bronze Age occupation; the Swedish excavations of the 1920s studied it.

lugares/dimini/resumen.texto: Settlement in Thessaly, near Iolcos, with Neolithic occupation and a Mycenaean tholos tomb. The Late Neolithic Dimini culture is placed around 5000 BC.

lugares/yolco/resumen.texto: Site in Thessaly, north of the Pagasetic Gulf, with a Bronze Age center; Greek tradition makes it the starting point of the Argonauts, and it was ruined in 294 BC when Demetrias was founded.

lugares/egina-kolonna/resumen.texto: Settlement on the island of Aegina, the island's largest Early Bronze Age settlement, fortified and built of stone; in the Middle Bronze Age it received Minoan pottery. It was the most important Early Bronze Age settlement on the island; there is Minoan pottery from c. 2000 BC.

lugares/lefkandi/resumen.texto: Settlement on the coast of Euboea in the Euripus strait, with cemeteries and a settlement at Xeropolis, occupied from the Bronze Age to the Dark Age.

lugares/micenas/resumen.texto: Citadel of the Argolid that gave its name to Mycenaean civilization. It was one of the great centers of Greece in the 2nd millennium BC, with its Lion Gate, shaft graves and tholos tombs.

lugares/puerta-de-los-leones/resumen.texto: Main entrance of the Mycenae citadel, c. 1250 BC, crowned by a relief of two lionesses; it is the only surviving monumental Mycenaean sculpture and the largest from the Aegean Bronze Age.

lugares/circulo-de-tumbas-a/resumen.texto: Cemetery of six shaft graves inside the Mycenae citadel, which Schliemann excavated in 1876; they held gold masks, weapons and jewelry of the 16th century BC.

lugares/circulo-de-tumbas-b/resumen.texto: Shaft grave cemetery outside the Mycenae citadel, older than Grave Circle A, excavated since 1951.

lugares/tesoro-de-atreo/resumen.texto: Tholos tomb at Mycenae, built between 1300 and 1250 BC, with an entrance corridor and a vaulted chamber 13 m high; later tradition gave it its name.

lugares/tumba-de-clitemnestra/resumen.texto: Tholos tomb at Mycenae, from the 13th century BC. Its name comes from later tradition, with no documented connection to the figure.

lugares/tirinto/resumen.texto: Mycenaean citadel of the Argolid, 20 km from Mycenae, with cyclopean walls and a palace with a megaron. It reached its greatest importance between 1400 and 1200 BC.

lugares/midea/resumen.texto: Mycenaean citadel of Argolis, with cyclopean walls, above the present village of the same name. Its first megaron dates to Late Helladic IIIB2 and it was destroyed around 1200 BC.

lugares/dendra/resumen.texto: Archaeological site in Argolid, next to the village of the same name, known for its Late Bronze Age cemetery: Persson excavated an intact tholos there and many Mycenaean chamber tombs, and in one of them the Panoply of Dendra, the oldest surviving bronze armour, was found in 1960.

lugares/prosimna/resumen.texto: Mycenaean site in Argolid with chamber tombs, between Mycenae and Argos, excavated by Blegen in the 1920s.

lugares/argos/resumen.texto: City of Argolid with continuous occupation since the Neolithic, in which the Mycenaean period precedes the historical city.

lugares/palacio-de-nestor/resumen.texto: Mycenaean palace at Ano Englianos, in Messenia, excavated from 1939 by Blegen; it held hundreds of Linear B tablets. Its destruction by fire is dated c. 1180 BC.

lugares/pilos-griffin/resumen.texto: Late Helladic pit grave, c. 1450 BC, near the palace of Nestor, with a warrior and more than 3 500 objects, among them the Pylos Combat Agate; it was excavated in 2015.

lugares/vafio/resumen.texto: Site in Laconia on the banks of the Eurotas, with a tholos tomb excavated in 1889 by Tsountas, from which the Vapheio cups come.

lugares/menelaion/resumen.texto: Sanctuary in the Peloponnese near Sparta, where a Late Helladic Mycenaean mansion precedes the historical cult of Menelaus and Helen.

lugares/gla/resumen.texto: Mycenaean fortress in Boeotia, on an island in Lake Copais, more than ten times larger than Tiryns; it is not mentioned in the Iliad.

lugares/orcomeno/resumen.texto: City of Boeotia occupied since the Neolithic, with a Mycenaean tholos tomb; Greek tradition associates it with the Minyans.

lugares/tebas-de-beocia/resumen.texto: City of Boeotia with continuous occupation; on the Cadmea there was a Mycenaean palace, with Linear B tablets and objects of gold, lapis lazuli and ivory.

lugares/cadmea/resumen.texto: Acropolis of Thebes, in Boeotia, with remains of a Mycenaean palace and Linear B tablets. Inhabited since at least the Early Bronze Age; its history can only be dated with certainty from the Late Mycenaean period, c. 1400 BC.

lugares/eleusis/resumen.texto: Site in Attica with Bronze Age occupation and a Mycenaean sanctuary that precedes the one of Demeter.

lugares/toricos/resumen.texto: Site in Attica, near the Laurion mines, with a Mycenaean tholos tomb.

lugares/brauron/resumen.texto: Site in Attica with Bronze Age occupation and later a sanctuary of Artemis.

lugares/nijoria/resumen.texto: Settlement in Messenia, with a continuous sequence from the Bronze Age to the Dark Age.

lugares/pellana/resumen.texto: Site in Laconia, in the Eurotas valley, which according to its excavator was the Mycenaean capital of Laconia; there are ancient tombs that tradition associates with Menelaus and Helen.

lugares/elatea/resumen.texto: City of Phocis with occupation from the Early Helladic period to Roman times. The occupation of the valley has been continuous since c. 6000 BC.

lugares/kalapodi/resumen.texto: Sanctuary in Phocis, with a sequence from the Bronze Age to the Classical period.

lugares/mileto/resumen.texto: City on the Ionian coast of Anatolia, with Bronze Age occupation, which in the Mycenaean period was under Aegean influence; Hittite texts call it Millawanda.

lugares/ialiso/resumen.texto: Site on the island of Rhodes with a Bronze Age settlement and necropolis, with a Mycenaean presence.

lugares/vatipetro/resumen.texto: Minoan site 4 km south of Archanes, in Crete, with some of the oldest wine presses in the world.

lugares/tumba-de-egisto/resumen.texto: Tholos tomb near the citadel of Mycenae, from Late Helladic IIA, c. 1510-1450 BC. Its name is traditional and it is not linked to the figure of Aegisthus.

lugares/kamilari/resumen.texto: Minoan necropolis with a tholos tomb, 1.9 km southwest of Agia Triada, where hundreds of vessels were found and, in Late Minoan IIIA tombs, clay models of a dance and of a banquet.
