lugares/apesokari/resumen.texto: Minoan necropolis of southern Mesara with two Early Minoan tholos tombs, first excavated in 1942.

lugares/kumasa/resumen.texto: Minoan site in southern Crete, known for its large pre-palatial cemetery, excavated by Xanthoudides between 1904 and 1906.

lugares/volimidia/resumen.texto: Site in Messenia with a cemetery of 35 tombs, mostly chamber tombs, from the end of the Middle Bronze Age, and a settlement from Late Helladic I to c. 1180 BC. It has been proposed as the religious centre of Sphagianes, in the territory of the palace of Nestor.

lugares/iaso/resumen.texto: City of Caria, on the Gulf of Güllük, Anatolia, with Bronze Age occupation, before the Greek city.

lugares/achladia/resumen.texto: Minoan villa site in eastern Crete, south of Sitia, excavated by Nikolaos Platon since 1939, with a large house of 270 m² and a smaller one. Platon dated it to Middle Minoan III, and his son Lefteris Platon, on other evidence, takes it to the Late Minoan period. For Nicolas Platon the villa is Middle Minoan III; another excavator believes it is Late Minoan.

lugares/apodoulou/resumen.texto: Minoan mansion or ceremonial building above the Libyan Sea, at 450 m altitude, excavated by Marinatos in 1934. It was in use in Middle Minoan III and yielded inscriptions in Linear A and a small gold axe. The building was in use in Middle Minoan III; the area has been inhabited since the Late Neolithic.

lugares/armenoi/resumen.texto: Minoan cemetery on the north coast of Crete, south of Rethymno, with 232 chamber tombs and one tholos, used mainly in Late Minoan II-IIIB. It is considered the most intact Minoan cemetery ever excavated; a stirrup jar with the text «wi-na-jo» in Linear B suggests Mycenaean contact.

lugares/agia-fotia/resumen.texto: Fortified Minoan building in eastern Crete, 5 km from Sitia, with 37 rooms around a courtyard, built in the period of the first palaces with a defensive wall. 150 m away is the Glyphada cemetery, with more than 250 Minoan chamber tombs.

lugares/kavusi-kastro/resumen.texto: Dark Age refuge settlement on a peak in eastern Crete, founded at the beginning of Late Minoan IIIC (12th century BC) and occupied without interruption until the Protogeometric period. Harriet Boyd explored it in 1900.

lugares/odigitria/resumen.texto: Minoan religious complex of two tholos tombs in the Asterousia mountains, in southern Crete, used from Early Minoan I to Middle Minoan IA. It was excavated in 1979-1980 and yielded seals, necklaces, gold diadems and stone vessels.

lugares/papoura/resumen.texto: Large Minoan architectural complex of concentric circles, about 48 m in diameter, on the top of Papoura hill, near Kastelli, in Crete. It was discovered in 2024 and was used mainly between 2000 and 1700 BC.

lugares/filaki/resumen.texto: Late Minoan IIIA tholos tomb, discovered in 1981 near a village in Crete, with at least nine burials and objects such as a gold necklace, fifteen seals and ivories with boar's-tusk helmets.

lugares/prassa/resumen.texto: Minoan settlement in Crete with two Middle Minoan houses that remained in use until Late Minoan I.

lugares/stravomyti/resumen.texto: Cave on the southwest slope of Mount Juktas, at 400 m altitude, used since the Neolithic as a shelter and burial place and then, from the Early Minoan period, for storage and worship. It may have been a sanctuary of a female deity. It was already used in the Neolithic as a shelter and burial place; later there was habitation, storage and worship.

lugares/tripiti/resumen.texto: Minoan settlement on a hill on the southern coast of the Mesara, with 36 rooms from Early Minoan II to Middle Minoan IA, excavated in 1986-1988.

lugares/troullos/resumen.texto: Eastern sector of the Minoan settlement of Archanes, in use from Middle Minoan II to Late Minoan I, with courtyards, multi-storey buildings and wall paintings. Evans, Marinatos and the Sakellarakis excavated it.

lugares/yerokambos/resumen.texto: Minoan cemetery in central southern Crete, near Lendas, with Early Minoan I tombs in use until Middle Minoan IA.

lugares/petsofas/resumen.texto: Minoan peak sanctuary in eastern Crete, associated with Palaikastro, used from Middle Minoan I to the Neopalatial period. It was the first Cretan peak sanctuary excavated systematically, by John Myres in 1903.

lugares/traostalos/resumen.texto: Minoan peak sanctuary in eastern Crete, excavated from 1963-1964 by Kostis Davaras, with clay human and animal figurines and a female figure with a swollen leg.

lugares/atsipades/resumen.texto: Open-air Minoan peak sanctuary in western Crete, on the summit of Atsipades Korakias, discovered in 1985 by K. Nowicki. The sanctuary was used between c. 2300 and 1700 BC.

lugares/vrysinas/resumen.texto: Minoan peak sanctuary on a peak south of Rethymno, the westernmost known Minoan site apart from Chania. It yielded a Linear A inscription on a stone table and miniature vessels.

lugares/trapeza/resumen.texto: Sacred cave of Crete from the Neolithic and the Bronze Age, described as a funerary cave; its pottery is similar to that of Knossos and Vasiliki.

lugares/sisi/resumen.texto: Important Minoan site about 500 m west of the present village on the north coast of Crete, showing occupation from before Early Minoan IIA.

lugares/cueva-de-ilitia/resumen.texto: Sacred cave of Crete dedicated to Eileithyia, goddess of childbirth, one kilometer from Amnisos. It was used from the Neolithic until c. 400 BC, and the cult flourished in the Late Minoan period. It was used from the Neolithic to Roman times, with the cult at its height in the Late Minoan period.

lugares/chamaizi/resumen.texto: Site in eastern Crete with the only known oval building of the Minoan period, from Middle Minoan IA, built around a cistern on Early Minoan foundations. Xanthoudidis excavated it in 1903.

lugares/priniatikos-pirgos/resumen.texto: Site on a coastal promontory in eastern Crete, settled from the Final Neolithic, c. 3000 BC, with occupation during the Minoan Bronze Age and into the Venetian period.

lugares/agios-vasileios/resumen.texto: Site of a Mycenaean palace 10 km south of Sparta, with light occupation in Early Helladic I-II, a palace built in Late Helladic IIIA, destroyed by fire in IIIB, partly rebuilt and destroyed again shortly afterwards.

lugares/lambayanna/resumen.texto: Submerged Early Helladic fortified settlement in the bay of Kiladha, in Argolid, at a depth of between 1 and 3 m. Its main phase is Early Helladic II, and it was discovered by chance in 2014.

lugares/mavrovouni/resumen.texto: Hill near Gytheio, in Laconia, settled since the Early Bronze Age, with seven rock-cut Mycenaean chamber tombs, a tholos and a Mycenaean settlement.

lugares/pavlopetri/resumen.texto: Submerged settlement in the bay of Vatika, in southern Laconia, with an almost complete plan of streets, buildings and tombs. It was thought to be Mycenaean, but later studies show occupation from c. 3500 BC; it is believed to have sunk around 1000 BC because of an earthquake.

lugares/tholos-de-kazarma/resumen.texto: Mycenaean tholos tomb in Argolid, from Late Helladic IIA, around 1500-1450 BC, on the road from Epidaurus to Argos; it is thought to have belonged to a local elite that controlled that route.

lugares/voudeni/resumen.texto: Mycenaean cemetery of 78 rock-cut tombs and a prehistoric settlement 7 km from Patras, in Achaea, one of the main sites on the periphery of the Mycenaean world. The settlement lasted about five hundred years (1500-1050 BC).

lugares/mitrou/resumen.texto: Tidal islet in the Gulf of Atalanti, in Locris, with a settlement occupied from the Neolithic and during the Bronze Age and the Early Iron Age, and a Bronze Age boat. Its occupation continues without interruption after the end of the Mycenaean palaces.

lugares/tzanata/resumen.texto: Village in southeast Cephalonia, in the locality of Broutzi, where Lazaros Kolonas found a Mycenaean tholos tomb 6.80 m in diameter in 1991. Tholos tomb of c. 1400 BC.

lugares/roca/resumen.texto: Site on the Adriatic coast of Apulia, in southern Italy, with very well preserved monumental Bronze Age architecture and the largest assemblage of Mycenaean pottery found west of mainland Greece.

lugares/berbati/resumen.texto: Valley in the northeast Peloponnese, northeast of Argos, excavated by the Swedish Institute at Athens since 1935 under the direction of Axel Persson. It had a Late Helladic potters' quarter with more than 175,000 pottery fragments. The first large settlement in the valley dates to the Early and Middle Neolithic, c. 6000-4500 BC.

lugares/manika/resumen.texto: Euboean city of Early Helladic II, 50 to 80 hectares, with an estimated 6 000 to 15 000 inhabitants, one of the largest Bronze Age settlements in Greece.

lugares/iklaina/resumen.texto: Late Bronze Age city (c. 1600-1100 BC) about 10 km northeast of Pylos, in Messenia, with an early Mycenaean palace, huge terrace walls, wall paintings, a drainage system and a fragmentary Linear B tablet from 1450-1350 BC.

lugares/teichos-dymaion/resumen.texto: Prehistoric acropolis in the territory of Dyme, in Achaea, occupied from c. 3500 BC and fortified in the Mycenaean period, probably around 1300 BC.

lugares/kukonisi/resumen.texto: Islet in the harbour of Moudros, on Lemnos, west of Poliochni, with the best-preserved Middle Bronze Age settlements, from 2000 to 1650 BC. Mycenaean pottery of the 13th century BC could indicate a permanent Greek settlement.

lugares/aigeira/resumen.texto: Site in northeastern Achaea, settled since the Middle Neolithic, c. 5500 BC, and excavated since 1916 by Austrian archaeologists. It was proposed as the centre of a possible Mycenaean state of Achaea, but no palatial structures or administration have been found.

lugares/cino/resumen.texto: Former main port of the Opuntian Locrians, at the northern end of the Opuntian Gulf, which appears in the Catalogue of Ships. The site, excavated between 1985 and 1995, has Bronze Age finds and, like others in the region, continuous occupation from the Mycenaean palatial period to the Early Iron Age.

lugares/eutresis/resumen.texto: Ancient village of Boeotia, mentioned in the Catalogue of Ships, near Thespiae. It gave its name to the Eutresis culture, the initial phase of the Bronze Age in mainland Greece. It gave its name to the Eutresis culture of Early Helladic I (c. 3200-2650 BC).
